name: Dash and action buffering
summary: Explicit buffering and cancellation rules let movement and combat form a learnable action grammar instead of competing for ignored inputs.
player_action: The player queues an attack, dash, aim, or follow-up while another movement or combat action is ending.
system_response: The game accepts, delays, cancels, or rejects the queued action according to visible state and stable priority rules.

weakened_by: animation events that drift from gameplay state
conflicts_with: uninterruptible commitment as the primary combat rule

failure_modes: A buffered action executes after the tactical reason for pressing it has passed.
Different weapons silently change action priority.
Invulnerability persists after an offensive cancellation.
Animation suggests a cancel window that gameplay does not accept.
accessibility: Allow longer buffer windows without changing enemy speed where possible.
Use visual and audio confirmation when an action is queued or unavailable.
Test button remapping and simultaneous inputs.

smallest_playable_test.setup: One weapon, one dash, one enemy tell, and a visible action-state timeline; test every ordered pair of movement and combat inputs near transition boundaries.
smallest_playable_test.retain_if: Players can predict the next action and use buffering without accidental late execution or invulnerability leakage.
smallest_playable_test.revise_if: Flow improves but particular transition pairs remain inconsistent.
smallest_playable_test.reject_if: The rules erase intended commitment or routinely execute tactically obsolete inputs.

evidence.claim: Hades post-launch patch notes explicitly improve attack input buffering to permit dashing between strikes and improve buffering after dash-strikes.
Hades patch notes correct dash invulnerability persisting after canceling into an attack.
evidence.notes: Demonstrates that cancellation and protection windows must be verified together.
